title: Dehumidifier Humidistat Settings by Room and Season
h1: What Should Your Dehumidifier Humidistat Be Set To?
dek: The EPA's 30–50% range is the fence, not the target. Here's the number to dial in for each room and season — and why the right number can still fail.
description: How to set a dehumidifier with a humidistat: the ideal humidity for basements, bedrooms, nurseries and bathrooms, plus seasonal adjustments and accuracy tips.
intro: A **dehumidifier with a humidistat** is only as good as the number you give it. For most rooms, set it between **40% and 50%** relative humidity, with **45%** as a dependable all-purpose default. Go a little lower in summer or in a room fighting mold or dust mites; nudge it a little higher in winter or in a bedroom where lower settings feel dry.

Get it wrong and you pay either way. Set too high, mold and dust mites move in while the unit still adds to your power bill. Set too low, the compressor runs nonstop chasing a target the room can't reach, wearing out the machine for no real benefit. The EPA's 30–50% recommendation marks the outer boundary; the real value comes from choosing the right number inside it for each room and season.

blocks.title: Special cases
blocks.text: Grow tents, greenhouses, root cellars and instrument rooms follow their own rules. A produce cellar, for example, actually wants humidity in the 80s — the opposite end of the dial. Check the specific guide before applying this chart.
Humid outdoor air leaks in through doors, windows and gaps, so you need the lower end of the range just to hold steady.
Winter: ease up or switch off

Heated air is naturally drier. Holding indoor humidity above about 40% during a cold snap can fog windows and, in cold climates, push moisture into exterior walls. Many HVAC sources suggest letting it drift toward 30–35% when it's below freezing outside. Our [window condensation guide](/guides/dehumidifier-for-condensation-on-windows/) has thresholds by outdoor temperature.
Shoulder seasons rarely need adjustment from the all-purpose 45% default.

Budget units often have a manual dial — Low, Medium, High or a few unlabeled marks — that can drift several points off true humidity over a year or two. That's fine in a garage or unfinished basement where a little slack doesn't matter. A digital humidistat displays and holds an exact percentage and is generally more accurate, which matters most in rooms with a narrow target, like a nursery.

items.label: Choose digital for living spaces
items.text: Bedrooms, nurseries and wood-floored rooms benefit from an exact, adjustable number.

items.label: Verify with a hygrometer
items.text: A separate humidity gauge placed across the room confirms the built-in reading.

items.label: Recheck yearly
items.text: If the built-in reading and your hygrometer disagree by more than a few points, trust the hygrometer and adjust the setpoint.

sections.heading: When the setting is right but the room isn't

blocks.text: A correct number only works if the unit is reading the room accurately and can actually reach the target. Three things commonly break that link:

items: **Sensor drift.** After a year or more, the internal sensor can read several points high or low, so the unit stops early or runs too long. Compare against a standalone hygrometer.
**Undersizing.** A unit too small for the moisture load runs nonstop and never reaches the setpoint. Check capacity with our [size guide](/guides/dehumidifier-size-guide/).
**Poor placement.** Tucked into a corner, a unit can sense its own exhaust instead of the room. Our [placement guide](/guides/where-to-place-a-dehumidifier/) covers clearances.
**No water in the bucket?** That's usually a different fault — see [dehumidifier not collecting water](/guides/dehumidifier-not-collecting-water/).

blocks.text: Start at **45%** for most rooms, drop to **40%** for a basement with an active moisture problem, and allow up to **50%** in winter or in bedrooms where lower settings feel dry. Lower it in summer, raise it or switch off in winter, and verify the reading with a separate hygrometer. A correctly set humidistat can still fail quietly if the sensor drifts, the unit is undersized or it's poorly placed.

faqs.q: What is a dehumidifier with a humidistat?
faqs.a: It's a dehumidifier with a built-in humidity sensor and control that lets you set a target, such as 45%. The unit runs until the room reaches that level, then cycles off and restarts when humidity climbs again. Units without one simply run until you turn them off or the tank fills.

faqs.q: What should I set my dehumidifier to in a basement?
faqs.a: About 45% for most basements. Start at 40% if there's visible condensation or a musty smell, then ease back toward 45% once the space stabilizes.

faqs.q: What humidity setting is best for a bedroom?
faqs.a: Around 45–50%. That's low enough for dust mites to die off over about a week or two, but not so low that it dries out your skin and sinuses overnight.

faqs.q: Should I change my humidistat setting in winter?
faqs.a: Yes. Heated air is drier, and holding humidity above about 40% in cold weather can cause window condensation. Many homes can lower the target to 30–35% or switch the dehumidifier off once it's freezing outside.

faqs.q: Why does my dehumidifier run constantly at the right setting?
faqs.a: Usually the sensor has drifted, the unit is too small for the space, or it's placed where it reads its own exhaust. Check the room with a separate hygrometer and review sizing and placement.

faqs.q: Is a digital humidistat more accurate than a dial?
faqs.a: Generally, yes. A digital humidistat displays and holds an exact percentage, while a manual dial has coarse settings and can drift over time.
